priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: The Trophy Twins
case.hook: Dr. Priya Nair here. The Duck Derby’s little brass trophy never reached the winner: it vanished from the judges’ table. Now TWO matching trophies sit at the Palmetto Springs lost-and-found. One is real brass. One is a painted plastic copy from the party store.

shelf.label: The lost-and-found shelf

trophies.line: Turned in Sunday, 4:10 p.m., by a jogger
Turned in Monday, 9:05 a.m., in a paper bag

shelf.note: The counter vote: almost everyone picked Trophy B. “It just looks newer and shinier.”

notice.head: PALMETTO SPRINGS LOST & FOUND
notice.title: Lost property report
rows: Small brass trophy cup, two handles
None. The engraving was not done yet
notice.line: Please send a scientist. We are not allowed to cut them open.

envelopes.front: Open when the real trophy is found
envelopes.head: The engraver’s note
envelopes.inside: I always weigh a trophy before I engrave it. The real brass cup is 412 grams exactly. — R. Vega, engraver
envelopes.verdict: Trophy A weighed 412 grams on your balance. It matches!

case.envLine: The engraver left a sealed note at the counter. Crack the case to open it.
case.question: Which trophy is the real brass one, and how can you prove it without cutting them open?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.where: Warm-Up: the bottle that fights back
clues.t: Stuff can be real even when you can’t see it. The capped bottle would not squash, because the trapped air inside takes up space and pushes back.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the matter gates
clues.t: Matter must pass BOTH tests: it has mass AND it takes up space. A rock, water and air all pass. A shadow and a sound fail.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: tell the twins apart
clues.t: Eyes can tie. The twin jars matched on every observable property. Only a measurement, mass, told them apart.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: the weigh and dunk test
clues.t: Both trophies pushed the water up the SAME 150 milliliters, but Trophy A has 412 grams of mass and Trophy B only 165. Different stuff inside.

solve.title: Which trophy is the real brass one?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Trophy B. It looks newer and shinier, and most people at the counter picked it.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Eyes can tie! Every observable property matched. Looking newer is not proof.

options.t: Trophy A. Both trophies take up the same space, but A has far more mass. Brass packs more stuff into the same space than painted plastic.
options.why: Case cracked! Same volume, very different mass: Trophy A must be made of heavier stuff. That is brass. And nobody had to cut anything open.

options.t: Trophy A, because it is bigger than Trophy B.
options.why: Check Clue 4. The dunk test: both trophies pushed the water up the SAME amount. They are the same size.

options.t: You can’t tell without cutting them open.
options.why: Check Clues 3 and 4. The balance and the tank told the twins apart from the outside.

squeeze.title: The bottle that fights back

why.t: An “empty” bottle is really full of air. The trapped air shows it is there by pushing back.

todo: Put the cap on. Drag down on the bottle to squeeze it, or press Squeeze it.
Take the cap off and squeeze again.
Watch your squeeze log. Then answer the question.
squeeze.model: A model bottle. Try it for real with a clean, empty plastic bottle.
squeeze.alt: A model plastic bottle on a table. A red cap can go on or off. Squeeze the bottle and watch what happens.
squeeze.dragHint: Drag down on the bottle to squeeze it yourself, or press Squeeze it.
squeeze.needBoth: Now try it with the cap {k}.

on: It dented a little, then sprang right back.
off: It squashed flat. The air whooshed out the top.

squeeze.q: The bottle looked empty. What pushed back when the cap was on?

opts.t: The air trapped inside. It takes up space, so there was no room to squash the bottle.
The plastic is just too stiff to squash.
opts.miss: Look at your log. With the cap OFF, the same plastic squashed flat.

opts.t: Nothing. The bottle was empty.
opts.miss: Something stopped your squeeze when the cap was on. The only thing inside was air.

squeeze.win: Trapped air pushed back! Air is invisible, but it is really there: it takes up space. Clue 1!

gates.afterText: Send them through the two tests.
gates.title: The matter gates

why.t: Two tests decide if something is matter: does it have mass, and does it take up space? Only things that pass BOTH gates come out as matter.

todo: Tap a thing to send it into the machine.
At each gate, pick the proof that answers the question.
Pass both gates: MATTER. Fail one: NOT MATTER. Test all five.

g1.sub: Would it press down on a scale?

g2.sub: Does it fill room that nothing else can use?

gates.pickLine: Tap the next thing to send it into the machine.

cands.name: A rock

opts.t: Yes. Put it on a scale and the number climbs.
Yes, because it is gray.
opts.miss: Gray is a color your eyes notice. Which proof uses a SCALE?

opts.t: Yes. Drop it in water and the water level climbs.
No. It is too small to take up space.
opts.miss: Small still counts! What happens to the water when a rock goes in?

cands.why: A rock has mass and takes up space. Matter.

cands.name: A cup of water

opts.t: Yes. A full cup weighs more than an empty cup.
No. Water is too runny to weigh.
opts.miss: Runny things still press on a scale. Compare a full cup and an empty cup.

opts.t: Yes. It fills the cup. Nothing else can use that room.
No. You can put your finger in it.
opts.miss: Your finger PUSHES the water out of the way. The water level climbs!

cands.why: Water has mass and fills space. Matter.

cands.name: Air in a balloon

opts.t: Yes. A blown-up balloon weighs a tiny bit more than an empty one.
No. You can’t see air, so it can’t have mass.
opts.miss: Seeing is not the test. The scale is. What did the Warm-Up bottle tell you?

opts.t: Yes. The capped bottle would not squash. The air filled the room inside.
No. Air is invisible, so it takes up no room.
opts.miss: Invisible is not the test. Remember what pushed back in the Warm-Up.

cands.why: Air has a little mass and takes up space. Matter, even though you can’t see it.

cands.name: A shadow

opts.t: No. A shadow on a scale changes nothing.
Yes. Big shadows are heavy.
opts.miss: Try it! Stand so your shadow falls on a scale. Does the number move?

cands.why: A shadow is just a spot where light is blocked. No mass, no space. Not matter.

cands.name: A bell’s ring

opts.t: No. A ringing room weighs the same as a quiet room.
Yes. Loud sounds are heavier than quiet ones.
opts.miss: Can you pour a sound into a cup or set it on a scale? Loud is not heavy.

cands.why: Sound is a wave traveling through matter (you learned that last week!), but the sound itself has no mass and fills no space. Not matter.

gates.q: What must be true, BOTH at once, for something to be matter?

opts.t: It has mass AND it takes up space.
You can see it and touch it.
opts.miss: Air passed both gates, and you can’t see air. Which two tests did the gates ask?

opts.t: It is heavy and hard.
opts.miss: A feather and water passed the same tests a rock did. The tests are about mass and space, not heavy and hard.

gates.win: Both tests, every time: mass AND space. That is what matter means. Clue 2!

airscale.title: Air on the scale
todo: Weigh the empty balloon.
Pump it up.
Weigh it again and watch the number.

why.t: Pump extra air into a balloon and you squeeze more matter inside. A good scale can feel it.

airscale.model: A model of a real balloon test.
airscale.alt: A model digital kitchen scale and a red balloon.
airscale.weighBtn: ⚖️ Put the balloon on the scale
airscale.pumpLine: Pumped full! Now weigh it again.
airscale.weigh2Line: Blown-up balloon: {x} g. The number climbed!
airscale.q: The scale climbed from 2.0 to 2.3 grams. What does the extra 0.3 grams prove?

opts.t: The air you pumped in has mass. Air is real matter.
The balloon got heavier because it stretched.
opts.miss: Stretching does not add stuff. What did the pump push INTO the balloon?

opts.t: The scale made a mistake.
opts.miss: Scientists have done this test many times, very carefully. The number climbs every time.

airscale.done: Wow! A scale can weigh air. Invisible does not mean nothing.

twins.afterText: but only one weighs 500 grams and only one is heavier than water.
twins.title: Tell the twins apart

why.t: Dr. Nair keeps twin practice jars, sealed just like the trophies. Which kind of property can split a tie your eyes can’t?

todo: Drag a tool onto the jars, or tap the tool and then the jars.
Each tool checks BOTH jars and adds a row to the table.
Try all four tools. Then answer the question.
twins.alt: Two sealed jars that look exactly alike, labeled Jar A and Jar B.
twins.dropHint: Each tool checks both jars at once.
twins.againMiss: You already used that tool. Try one with no check mark.

tools.note: A measurement can tie too. Keep going.
There it is! The balance broke the tie.

twins.q: The jars looked, felt and measured the same height. What finally told them apart?

opts.t: A measurable property: their mass, in grams.
An observable property: one looked newer.
opts.miss: Check the table. Every LOOK and FEEL row says SAME.

opts.t: Nothing can tell twins apart.
opts.miss: One row says DIFFERENT! Which tool made that row?

twins.win: When eyes tie, numbers decide. A measured property split the twins. Clue 3!

dunklab.afterText: weigh each one, then hold it under the water and watch how far the water climbs.
dunklab.title: The weigh and dunk test

why.t: When something goes all the way under, it shoves water aside, so the water line climbs exactly as much space as it takes up.

todo: Put each trophy on the balance and read the screen.
Hold each trophy under the water with the rod. Read how far the water climbs.
Fill both property cards. Then compare them.
dunklab.model: A model lab bench. The rod holds the trophy under the water.
dunklab.alt: A model balance scale and a measuring tank with a push rod, used to measure each trophy.

massOpts.miss: Look again at the number on the scale screen.
Look again at the number on the scale screen.

volOpts.miss: Where did the water start, and where is the line now? Count the marks.
Where did the water start, and where is the line now? Count the marks.

massOpts.miss: Look again at the number on the scale screen.
That was Trophy A. Read this screen.

volOpts.miss: Count the marks. It climbed just as far as Trophy A did.
Count the marks. It climbed just as far as Trophy A did.

dunklab.readScale: Read the screen. What is the mass?
dunklab.readTank: How far did the water climb?
dunklab.doneLine: Both cards are full. Read them side by side.
dunklab.q: Same volume, very different mass. What does that tell you about the trophies?

opts.t: They take up the same space but are made of different stuff. One packs much more matter into the same room.
Trophy A is bigger than Trophy B.
opts.miss: Check the volume rows. The water climbed the SAME amount for both.

opts.t: The balance must be broken.
opts.miss: The balance read the twin jars just fine. Two true measurements can be different.

dunklab.win: You measured mass AND volume, and the numbers cracked it open: same space, different stuff. Clue 4!

kgsphere.title: The most careful measuring on Earth
todo: Look at the real photo.
Then answer the question.
kgsphere.alt: A scientist in a white coat and white gloves holds a dark, mirror-shiny silicon sphere about the size of a grapefruit.
kgsphere.cap: A real, nearly perfect silicon sphere. Scientists polished it for years so its mass could help pin down exactly what one kilogram is. Photo: CSIRO, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
kgsphere.q: Why would scientists spend YEARS polishing one perfect ball?

opts.t: To pin down exactly how much matter one kilogram is, so every scale on Earth can agree.
Because shiny balls are worth a lot of money.
opts.miss: It is not for selling. Think about what every scale in the world needs to agree on.

opts.t: To use it as a mirror.
opts.miss: It is shiny, but that is not the job. What property were they pinning down?

kgsphere.fact: You used the same idea today: when looks can’t settle it, careful measuring can. Yours took one afternoon. Theirs took years.
kgsphere.win: From a lost trophy to a perfect sphere: measuring matter settles arguments.

tool.name: Pan balance
tool.teaser: Weigh pairs on a two-pan balance. Then find the heavy box in just two weighings.
tool.done: You balanced it! A pan balance sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: One of the oldest measuring tools in the world. Put something on each pan: the heavier side sinks. When the pans sit level, both sides hold the same mass.

panbalance.title: Which side sinks?
todo: Tap an object, then tap again to load the other pan. Press Weigh them.
Weigh two different pairs.
Then try the two-weighings puzzle.
panbalance.model: A model balance. When the pans sit level, the two sides have the same mass.
panbalance.trayLabel: The tray (tap one object for the left pan, then one for the right)
panbalance.tipLine: The {a} side sank: more mass, even when it is not bigger.
panbalance.pairLine: Weigh one more pair. Can the BIGGER thing lose?

puzzle.head: The two-weighings puzzle
puzzle.sub: Three boxes look exactly alike. One is heavier inside. You may weigh only TWICE. Find it!
puzzle.balLine: {a} and {b} balance. Neither one is the heavy box.
puzzle.ask: Which box is the heavy one?

opts.t: Box 1
opts.miss: Check your weighings. Did Box 1 ever sink a pan?

opts.t: Box 2
Box 3
opts.miss: Check your weighings. Did Box 3 ever sink a pan?

puzzle.done: Puzzle solved in two weighings or fewer!

q.q: The pans sit LEVEL. What does that tell you?

opts.t: The two sides hold the same mass.
The two sides are the same size.
opts.why: A balance feels mass, not size. A big sponge can balance a tiny stone.

opts.t: The balance is stuck.
opts.why: Level is an answer, not a jam: it means the two sides match.

q1.A: A shadow is just a dark spot where light is blocked. Run it through the two gates.
q1.B: Can you pour a sound into a jar, or set it on a scale? Think about the gates.

q2.A: A ruler measures how long something is. Which tool did the trophies sit on?
q2.C: A thermometer measures how hot. Which tool reads in grams?

q3.B: “Brown” is something your eyes notice: observable. Which option has a NUMBER?
q3.C: A smell has no number. Which option could you write in grams?

ans-3.label: what could go wrong with one

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-1: Pick one object. What do your eyes and fingers notice? What could a tool put a number on?
Observable: color, shape, texture. Measurable: mass in grams, volume, length.
Try: The ___ is ___ and ___. Its mass is about ___ and its length is about ___.
ans-3: Remember the twin jars. How many properties matched before one split them?
One property can tie, or fit LOTS of objects. More properties pin down one exact thing.
Try: Scientists list many properties because ___. With only one, ___ could happen.

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: The capped bottle would not squash: the trapped air inside pushed back.
The balloon made the scale climb from 2.0 to 2.3 grams.
Each trophy pushed the water line up 150 milliliters when it went under.
Almost everyone at the counter picked the shinier trophy.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

photos.afterText: a rock packed with tiny shells. Look closely:
photos.title: Florida limestone, up close
todo: Tap each number on the photo.
For each label, decide: observable, or would you need a tool?

why.t: A wall of the Castillo de San Marcos, a 350-year-old fort in St. Augustine. Its blocks are coquina: tiny shells pressed into rock.

photos.alt: A very close view of a coquina limestone wall: thousands of tiny tan shell pieces pressed together, with a smoother pale patch and small holes.
photos.credit: Kiran891, Castillo de San Marcos National Monument

hotspots.label: Tiny shells
hotspots.t: Thousands of little shell pieces, pressed together into rock. You can SEE them: an observable property.

hotspots.label: A smooth, pale patch
hotspots.t: Weather wore this spot smooth and lighter in color. Color and texture: observable properties.

hotspots.label: A little hole
hotspots.t: Water slowly dissolves limestone and leaves holes. In Florida’s ground, holes like this grow into springs and sinkholes.

task.q: Match it: which label shows each clue about this rock?

items.step: Tiny pieces pressed together into rock
items.evid: Coquina is made of tiny shells pressed together. You can SEE them: observable.
items.miss: Look for the spot crowded with little shell bits.

items.step: A patch with a different color and feel
items.evid: Weather wore one patch smooth and pale. Color and texture are observable properties.
items.miss: Look for the smoother, lighter spot.

items.step: Proof that water slowly eats limestone
items.evid: Water dissolves limestone and leaves holes. Big holes become Florida’s springs and sinkholes.
items.miss: Look for the dark little opening in the wall.

task.win: Good eye! A photo shows observable properties. For mass or volume you would still need tools, like today’s balance and tank.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · the bottle that fights back (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Dr. Nair here. Before we touch those trophies, squeeze a bottle. Put the cap on, then drag down on the bottle. Feel that push back? Now take the cap off and squeeze again. Watch your squeeze log fill in, and ask: what was pushing?

part1.label: Part 1 · the matter gates (Clue 2)
part1.script: Time to test, not guess. Tap the rock to send it into the machine. Gate one asks: does it have mass? Gate two: does it take up space? Pick your proof at each gate. The shadow and the bell might surprise you. Fill both trays.

explore.label: Part 3 · the weigh and dunk test (Clue 4)
explore.script: The real test. Put Trophy A on the balance and read the screen. Then hold it under the water with the rod, and read how far the water climbs. Do both trophies. When both property cards are full, compare them. Same space, different mass. What does that mean?

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says air takes up no space because you can’t see it. You tested that today! Pick your side, tap two facts in the planner, then write your reasoning. Claim, evidence, reasoning. That’s your C-E-R.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 27.02 (classify by properties, pick the right material for a job).

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell what matter is, or how a property can be observed or measured?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, even air you cannot see.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “matter”, “mass” and “space”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
